title: Two sticks (Ezekiel 37:15–28)
hook: the sticks of Judah and Joseph become one in the prophet's hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, a valley of dry bones, and a question: can these bones live? Breath came from the four winds, and they stood. Your line was can these bones live. What small step did you take? Today, the same chapter goes on, with two pieces of wood. Day eight hundred fifteen.

Two sticks. That's all Ezekiel needs for today's message. No vision this time, no fire, no wheels. Just two ordinary pieces of wood. He's told to write a name on each one. On the first: For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions. On the second: For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions. Two names that stood for the two kingdoms, south and north, and the north had been carried off and scattered. And then he's told to hold them.
screen: `TWO PIECES OF WOOD.` → `ONE FOR JUDAH, ONE FOR JOSEPH.` → `HOLD THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the instruction, in the King James words: "And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand." From where the people stand, it looks like this: two sticks, end to end, held in one fist. The prophet's hand closes around the seam. It's street theater, and it's meant to make people ask. So the text gives them their question: wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest by these? And the answer comes: God will take the stick of Joseph and join it with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine hand. Notice the shift. First, one in thy hand, the prophet's. Then, one in mine hand, God's. In the text, the prophet's small act pictures something God says he will finish. Then the promise is spelled out. The scattered will be gathered from among the nations and brought home. And this line: they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all. One king. One people. A covenant of peace. And God's dwelling place with them. Remember the north falling, a few weeks back, its people carried off to Assyria. This is where a prophet says the story isn't over. Jewish tradition carries the hope of gathering the scattered in its prayers. But the image also works at kitchen-table size. Two people who stopped speaking. Two halves of a family. Two parts of yourself that don't get along. The prophet doesn't glue the sticks. He holds them together in his hand, and waits for the rest.
screen: `WRITE A NAME ON EACH STICK.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BECOME ONE IN THINE HAND.` · then: `THY HAND, THEN MINE HAND.` · `NO MORE TWO KINGDOMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: join two divided things. If there's a pen, a spoon or a twig nearby, pick up two of them. If not, just open your hands. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two things that are split apart: two people, two sides of a family, two parts of your own life. Let one rest in each hand. Then, slowly, bring your hands together and hold them as one. Don't solve anything. Just feel what it's like to hold both. If you pray, you can place them in God's hand. The bell holds the time.
Two sticks. Ezekiel writes Judah on one and Joseph on the other, and holds them so they become one in his hand: a promise that the divided will be joined. Today's word.
Your line: one in thy hand. Today, do one small thing that brings two divided people, or two parts of your life, a little closer together. Day eight hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 37:15–28 as the prophetic reading for the Torah portion Vayigash, where Joseph and Judah meet, and the hope of gathering the scattered appears in daily prayer.

pairs: for Joseph, the stick of Ephraim

they ask: wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest by these?

the text says they shall be no more two nations, neither divided into two kingdoms.

fork.setup: you're Ezekiel, holding two sticks with two names on them. what are you told to do?
options: join them into one stick in your hand.
fork.reveal: he joins them so they become one in his hand, and then God says: they shall be one in mine hand.

original.note: Hebrew: wood, or a stick, the word Ezekiel writes the names on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet doing a strange trick with sticks.
what it means: the divided kingdoms of Judah and Joseph will be joined into one people.
what a scholar hears: one in thy hand becomes one in mine hand, a human gesture pointing to what God says he will finish.

notes: Ezekiel 37:15–28 as the haftarah for Vayigash appears in howItsDone; Keeper please confirm.
'a few weeks back' refers to day 777 (The north falls), which also previewed the two sticks.
The stick inscriptions in the hook paraphrase KJV 37:16 closely; Keeper may prefer JPS 1917 wording.
'Jewish tradition carries the hope of gathering the scattered in its prayers' refers to the weekday Amidah blessing for the ingathering of exiles.
Editor: cut 'and a pen' (the text only says write); reworded the look-back to day 777 so it doesn't claim Kings 'goes silent about the lost tribes'.
Audit: narrator's 'only God can finish' (a belief claim in the narrator's voice) now attributed to the text in teach and trapdoor; 'handed' fixed, since 37:16 has Ezekiel take the sticks himself.
